hints: Look closely at where the dark-stained chromosomes sit in each labelled cell - are they lined up in a single row in the middle or pulled apart toward two ends?
Recall which stage holds chromosomes on the spindle equator and which stage splits centromeres so sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
walkthrough:
Read the chromosome position in cell A**
In cell A the chromosomes form a dark line across the middle of the cell. That is the spindle equator, also called the metaphase plate. Holding all chromosomes in one central line is the hallmark of metaphase.

Read the chromosome position in cell B**
In cell B there are two dark groups of chromosomes moving apart toward opposite ends of the cell, with spindle microtubules visible between them. Separation of sister chromatids to opposite poles after centromere division is the hallmark of anaphase.
Final answer: A - metaphase; B - anaphase.

hints: Start from prophase - what structure made of microtubules is built between the two poles of the cell?
Think about where those fibres attach on each chromosome and how that attachment lets chromosomes be moved to the middle and held there.
Think about what must happen to those fibres in anaphase to pull one copy of each chromosome to each end so both nuclei get a full set.
walkthrough:
Build the spindle in prophase**
Microtubules polymerise to form the spindle apparatus stretching from pole to pole. This creates the tracks that will handle the chromosomes.

Attach and position chromosomes**
Spindle microtubules attach to the kinetochore at the centromere of each chromatid. They then move the chromosomes to the spindle equator and hold them on the metaphase plate during metaphase.

Separate chromatids in anaphase**
In anaphase the kinetochore microtubules shorten by disassembly, the centromeres divide, and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. Pole-to-pole fibres also lengthen to elongate the cell, so each end receives one identical chromatid of every chromosome.

Final answer: Microtubules form the spindle fibres; attach to centromere / kinetochore; move chromosomes to spindle equator and maintain them there in metaphase; in anaphase microtubules shorten, centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles so each daughter nucleus receives one chromatid of each chromosome.

hints: Cell C shows the chromosomes have already reached the poles - what is the next stage called when two new nuclei start to be rebuilt?
Think about what must reform around each chromosome group and what happens to the tightly coiled chromosomes and nucleolus.
Remember this is an animal embryo cell, so think how the cytoplasm itself is split - what pinches inward at the equator?
walkthrough:
Recognise telophase**
The chromosomes have finished moving apart. Now the cell reverses many prophase changes to make two separate nuclei. That is telophase.

Rebuild two nuclei**
A nuclear envelope reforms around each group of chromosomes. Inside, chromosomes uncoil and decondense back to chromatin, and the nucleolus reappears in each nucleus. Organelles are shared between the two halves.

Split the cytoplasm**
Cytokinesis follows. In animal cells a contractile ring of microfilaments pulls the cell surface membrane inward to form a cleavage furrow at the equator, pinching the cytoplasm into two separate daughter cells.

Final answer: Cell C is in telophase. Nuclear envelope reforms around each group of chromosomes; chromosomes uncoil / decondense to chromatin; nucleoli reform; cytokinesis occurs by formation of a cleavage furrow which pinches the cell into two.

hints: Start before mitosis in interphase - how is DNA copied so that each chromosome ends up with two identical DNA molecules?
Think about the events in metaphase and anaphase that guarantee each daughter cell gets exactly one copy of every chromosome, not two copies or none.
Think about the safety system of the cell cycle that stops the cell moving on if copying went wrong and allows repair to avoid mutation.
walkthrough:
Make identical copies**
During S phase of interphase, DNA replicates semi-conservatively. Each new chromatid is identical to the old one, so each chromosome consists of two identical DNA molecules joined at the centromere.

Share one copy with each daughter**
In metaphase all chromosomes align on the spindle equator. In anaphase centromeres split, spindle fibres shorten and identical sister chromatids move to opposite poles. Each daughter nucleus therefore receives one sister chromatid of every chromosome - a full identical set.

Check and repair**
Checkpoints in the cell cycle stop the cell entering the next stage if there are errors. This allows time for DNA polymerase to repair replication errors, so mutations are not passed to daughter cells and the daughters stay genetically identical.

Final answer: Semi-conservative DNA replication in interphase produces two identical sister chromatids per chromosome; chromosomes align on spindle equator in metaphase then sister chromatids separate to opposite poles in anaphase so each daughter receives one identical chromatid of each chromosome; checkpoints prevent progression if errors occur and allow repair by DNA polymerase, avoiding mutations.
